claim: Pathological loss-of-function mutations in cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD).
source: Pathological loss-of-function mutations in cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) (Weaving et al., 2004; Bahi-Buisson et al., 2012) cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD, OMIM 300203, 300672)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research establishing this causal relationship

claim: CDD has an incidence of 1:40,000–60,000.
source: a rare (incidence 1:40,000–60,000; Lindy et al., 2018; Kothur et al., 2018; Symonds, 2017) neurodevelopmental disorder
evidence: Supported by citations to epidemiological studies

claim: CDD is associated with severe early-life epilepsy, motor, cognitive, visual, and autonomic disturbances.
source: neurodevelopmental disorder associated with severe early-life epilepsy, motor, cognitive, visual, and autonomic disturbances (Bahi-Buisson et al., 2012; Bahi-Buisson et al., 2008; Nemos et al., 2009; Castrén et al., 2011; Melani et al., 2011; Fehr et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to clinical studies

claim: Epilepsy in CDD is very medically refractory.
source: Current experience demonstrates that epilepsy in CDD is very medically refractory (Müller et al., 2016; Demarest et al., 2019; Olson et al., 2019; Leonard et al., 2022; with rare exception [Aznar-Laín et al., 2023; MacKay et al., 2020])
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies with rare exceptions noted

claim: Ganaxolone provides modest improvements but not seizure freedom in CDD.
source: a newly approved therapy (ganaxolone, a neuroactive steroid that enhances GABAergic inhibition) provides modest improvements but not seizure freedom (Knight et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to clinical trial data

claim: Hemizygous males and heterozygous females can be equally and severely affected by CDD.
source: Hemizygous males and heterozygous females can be equally and severely affected (Demarest et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies

claim: CDD symptoms occur in the absence of any structural brain pathology.
source: These severe symptoms are in the absence of any structural brain pathology (Pini et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to neuroimaging studies

claim: CDKL5 kinase function is central to disease pathology in CDD.
source: Recent analysis of genetic variants in CDD has indicated that CDKL5 kinase function is central to disease pathology (Demarest et al., 2019; Hector et al., 2017b)
evidence: Supported by citations to genetic analysis studies

claim: Loss of kinase function seems functionally equivalent to loss of the CDKL5 protein.
source: In other words, loss of kinase function seems functionally equivalent to loss of the protein.
evidence: Inferred from genetic variant analysis mentioned in preceding sentence

claim: CDKL5 is expressed throughout the CNS primarily in neurons in rodent models.
source: In rodent models, CDKL5 is expressed throughout the CNS primarily in neurons, increases postnatally, and is stabilized at peak levels in adults (Chen et al., 2010; Hector et al., 2016; Baltussen et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to expression studies in rodent models

claim: CDKL5 expression increases postnatally and is stabilized at peak levels in adults in rodent models.
source: In rodent models, CDKL5 is expressed throughout the CNS primarily in neurons, increases postnatally, and is stabilized at peak levels in adults (Chen et al., 2010; Hector et al., 2016; Baltussen et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to developmental expression studies

claim: Adult rodent models of CDD are associated with abnormal behaviors and visual disturbances.
source: Adult rodent models of CDD are associated with abnormal behaviors, visual disturbances (Zhu and Xiong, 2019), and multiple abnormal signaling cascades (Wang et al., 2012; Fuchs et al., 2015; Fuchs et al., 2014; Schroeder et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to rodent model studies

claim: CDKL5 is localized to the dendritic spines of excitatory synapses as well as the nucleus of neurons.
source: CDKL5 is localized to the dendritic spines of excitatory synapses as well as the nucleus of neurons (Chen et al., 2010; Rusconi et al., 2008; Oi et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to subcellular localization studies

claim: CDKL5 functions in the formation of excitatory synapses with partners that include PSD-95, NGL-1, Shootin1, and actin.
source: CDKL5 functions in the formation of excitatory synapses with partners that include PSD-95 (Zhu et al., 2013), NGL-1 (Ricciardi et al., 2012), Shootin1 (Nawaz et al., 2016), and actin (Chen et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to protein interaction studies

claim: MAP1S and microtubule end binding protein 2 (EB2) are physiological CDKL5 substrates in brain.
source: Recent work has identified MAP1S and microtubule end binding protein 2 (EB2) as physiological CDKL5 substrates in brain (Baltussen et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to substrate identification study

claim: A phosphospecific antibody for EB2-S222 has been used to report CDKL5 activity in mouse models and human iPSCs.
source: A phosphospecific antibody for EB2-S222 has been used to report CDKL5 activity in mouse models and human iPSCs (Baltussen et al., 2018; Terzic et al., 2021; Di Nardo et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies using this antibody

claim: CDKL5 is a binding partner of both PSD-95 and gephyrin.
source: CDKL5 is a binding partner of both PSD-95 and gephyrin (Uezu et al., 2016; De Rosa et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to protein interaction studies

claim: Binding of CDKL5 with PSD-95 is critical for excitatory spine synapse development.
source: binding with PSD-95 is critical for excitatory spine synapse development (Wang et al., 2012) and maintenance of inhibitory synapses (De Rosa et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to functional studies

claim: Loss of CDKL5 leads to a global reduction in excitatory synapse numbers.
source: Studies have typically found that loss of CDKL5 leads to a global reduction in excitatory synapse numbers (Ricciardi et al., 2012; Della Sala et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to synapse quantification studies

claim: Loss of CDKL5 leads to reduced PSD-95 and synapsin.
source: reduced PSD-95 (Negraes et al., 2021; Lupori et al., 2019), and synapsin (Negraes et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to protein expression studies

claim: Loss of CDKL5 leads to loss of AMPA-type glutamate receptors (GluA2).
source: with loss of AMPA-type glutamate receptors (GluA2; Yennawar et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to receptor expression study

claim: Loss of CDKL5 leads to increased NMDA-type glutamate receptors (GluN2B).
source: and increased NMDA-type glutamate receptors (GluN2B; Okuda et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to receptor expression study

claim: Embryonic knock-out of Cdkl5 in rodents either enhanced long-term potentiation (LTP) or did not affect LTP in an age-dependent fashion.
source: Embryonic knock-out of Cdkl5 rodents either enhanced long-term potentiation (LTP) (Okuda et al., 2017; de Oliveira et al., 2022) or did not affect LTP (Yennawar et al., 2019; de Oliveira et al., 2022) in an age-dependent fashion
evidence: Supported by citations to electrophysiology studies showing variable results

claim: Immature CDKL5-deficient mice do not have seizures or epilepsy.
source: Further, immature CDKL5-deficient mice do not have seizures or epilepsy (Wang et al., 2012; Amendola et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to seizure phenotyping studies

claim: Immature CDKL5-deficient mice appear insensitive to pro-convulsants such as kainate.
source: and appear insensitive to pro-convulsants such as kainate (Wang et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to pharmacological challenge study

claim: CDKL5 is an X-linked gene encoding a 115 kDa serine-threonine kinase.
source: CDKL5 is an X-linked gene encoding a 115 kDa serine-threonine kinase and member of the CMGC family
evidence: Based on established knowledge of CDKL5 gene and protein characteristics

claim: CDKL5 is a member of the CMGC family that includes cyclin-dependent kinases (CDK), MAP-kinases, glycogen synthase kinases (GSK), and cyclin-dependent kinase-like (CDKL).
source: member of the CMGC family that includes cyclin-dependent kinases (CDK), MAP-kinases, glycogen synthase kinases (GSK), and cyclin-dependent kinase-like (CDKL) (Manning et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to kinase classification study

claim: CDKL5 has significant homology to GSK3β.
source: but significant homology to GSK3β (Davis et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to structural comparison study

claim: CDKL1-4 mRNA are expressed at much lower levels than CDKL5 in mouse and human brain.
source: CDKL1-4 mRNA are expressed at much lower levels than CDKL5 in mouse and human brain (http://mouse.brain-map.org)
evidence: Supported by reference to expression database

claim: GSK3α and GSK3β have been linked to brain synaptic function.
source: Of these kinases, only GSK3α (Shahab et al., 2014; Ebrahim Amini et al., 2022) and GSK3β Peineau et al., 2008 have been linked to brain synaptic function
evidence: Supported by citations to functional studies

claim: Cdkl5 knock-out mice have increased GSK3β activity.
source: Cdkl5 knock-out mice have increased GSK3β activity, as evidenced by hypo-phosphorylation of GSK3β at S-9 and decreased β-catenin (Fuchs et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to biochemical analysis study

claim: Inhibition of GSK3β in CDKL5 young but not old knock-out mice normalizes expression of β-catenin and S9-phospho-GSK3β.
source: Inhibition of GSK3β in CDKL5 (young but not old) knock-out mice normalizes expression of β-catenin and S9-phospho-GSK3β (Fuchs et al., 2015; Fuchs et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to pharmacological rescue studies

claim: Activation of GSK3β is required for the induction of GluN-LTD while inhibition occurs with the induction of LTP.
source: Activation of GSK3β is required for the induction of GluN-LTD while inhibition occurs with the induction of LTP (Peineau et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to electrophysiology study

claim: SNS-032 and AT-7519 were initially identified as potent CDK inhibitors.
source: SNS-032 and AT-7519 were initially identified as potent CDK inhibitors (Davis et al., 2011; Vasta et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to inhibitor characterization studies

claim: A plate of 25 compounds was assembled with IC50 < 400 nM in the CDKL5 NanoBRET assay and >20fold difference between the CDKL5 NanoBRET and the GSK3β NanoBRET IC50 values.
source: Based on the data generated, a plate of 25 compounds was assembled. The criteria for inclusion on this plate included an IC50 < 400 nM in the CDKL5 NanoBRET assay and >20fold difference between the CDKL5 NanoBRET and the GSK3β NanoBRET IC50 values (Table 1)
evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 1

claim: Almost all inhibitors showed a pSer222 EB2 reduction at 500 nM in rat primary cortical neurons.
source: Almost all inhibitors showed a pSer222 EB2 reduction at 500 nM; most inhibitors showed a reduction at 50 nM (Figure 1)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1

claim: Three inhibitors (CAF-382 (B1), HW2-013 (B4), and LY-213 (B12)) caused a significant reduction in pSer222 EB2 at 5 nM without a change in total EB2 levels.
source: Three inhibitors caused a significant reduction in pSer222 EB2 at 5 nM without a change in total EB2 levels: CAF-382 (B1), HW2-013 (B4), and LY-213 (B12) (Figure 1)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1

claim: B1 is an SNS-032 analog.
source: As shown in Figure 2, B1 is an SNS-032 analog
evidence: Supported by chemical structure shown in Figure 2

claim: B4 and B12 are analogs of AT-7519.
source: while B4 and B12 are analogs of AT-7519
evidence: Supported by chemical structures shown in Figure 2

claim: B1 has a selectivity score S10 (1 µM) = 0.017.
source: While B1 has a good selectivity score (S10 [1 µM] = 0.017; 7 kinases with PoC < 10 at 1 µM)
evidence: Supported by kinome profiling data shown in Figure 3A

claim: B1 potently inhibits CDK9, PCTK1/CDK16, PCTK2/CDK17, and PCTK3/CDK18 (IC50 ≤ 100 nM).
source: several CDKs (CDK9, PCTK1/CDK16, PCTK2/CDK17, PCTK3/CDK18) are potently inhibited (IC50 ≤ 100 nM) (colored green in the nested table in Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 3A

claim: B1 shows a 44-fold selectivity window between CDKL5 and CDK7.
source: Analysis of biochemical data reveals potent binding/inhibition of CDKL5, CDK9, CDK16, CDK17, and CDK18, and a 44-fold selectivity window between CDKL5 and the next most potently inhibited kinase (CDK7)
evidence: Inferred from IC50 values presented in Figure 3A

claim: Nearly 100-fold selectivity was observed for B1 for CDKL5 versus CDKL2.
source: When comparing the binding and enzymatic assay results, nearly 100-fold selectivity was observed for CDKL5 versus the most potently inhibited kinase, CDKL2
evidence: Supported by thermal shift and enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: B1 did not inhibit CDKL1.
source: and this compound did not inhibit CDKL1
evidence: Supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: B4 has a selectivity score S10(1 µM) = 0.02.
source: Compounds B4 and B12, which are analogs of AT-7519, also demonstrated good kinome-wide selectivity with S10(1 µM) scores of 0.02 and 0.01, respectively (Figure 3B and C)
evidence: Supported by kinome profiling data shown in Figure 3B

claim: B12 has a selectivity score S10(1 µM) = 0.01.
source: Compounds B4 and B12, which are analogs of AT-7519, also demonstrated good kinome-wide selectivity with S10(1 µM) scores of 0.02 and 0.01, respectively (Figure 3B and C)
evidence: Supported by kinome profiling data shown in Figure 3C

claim: B4 binds with high affinity to CDKL5, GSK3α, and GSK3β.
source: This orthogonal profiling of B4 confirmed high-affinity binding to CDKL5, GSK3α, and GSK3β (green in nested table in Figure 3B, curves in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2B)
evidence: Supported by binding and NanoBRET assay data shown in Figure 3B and supplements

claim: B12 binds with high affinity to CDKL5, GSK3α, and GSK3β.
source: Orthogonal profiling of B12 confirmed high-affinity binding to CDKL5, GSK3α, and GSK3β (green in nested table in Figure 3C, curves in Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2C)
evidence: Supported by binding and NanoBRET assay data shown in Figure 3C and supplements

claim: B12 is a more effective inhibitor of GSK3α when compared to GSK3β.
source: This compound is a more effective inhibitor of GSK3α when compared to GSK3β
evidence: Inferred from IC50 values presented in Figure 3C

claim: WT CDKL5 but not KD CDKL5 elicited kinase activity in the presence of ATP (50 µM).
source: We observed that, in the presence of ATP (50 µM, Figure 4A), WT CDKL5 but not KD CDKL5 elicited kinase activity, as measured by turnover of ATP to ADP via a luminescent reagent (ADP-Glo assay)
evidence: Supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 4A

claim: B1 and AST-487 robustly inhibited CDKL5 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: B1 and AST-487, however, robustly inhibited CDKL5 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4C and D)
evidence: Supported by kinase assay data shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: The difference between DMSO, lapatinib, and untreated CDKL5 was not significant at 10 or 100 nM.
source: The difference between DMSO, lapatinib, and untreated CDKL5 was not significant at 10 or 100 nM (Figure 4C and D)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of kinase assay data shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: CAF-382 (B1) showed a significant reduction in pSer222 EB2/total EB2 at 500 nM concentration in primary neurons.
source: We found that CAF-382 (B1) showed a significant reduction in pSer222 EB2/total EB2 at 500 nM concentration (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Phospho-β-catenin/total β-catenin was not changed by CAF-382 (B1) over the entire concentration range.
source: Phospho-β-catenin/total β-catenin was not changed over the entire concentration range, indicating that CAF-382 (B1) does not inhibit GSK3b (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A

claim: HW2-013 (B4) was effective in reducing EB2 pSer222 at 500 nM but also inhibited GSK3β significantly at 500 nM.
source: HW2-013 (B4) was effective in reducing EB2 pSer222 at 500 nM but also inhibited GSK3β significantly at 500 nM with a trend of inhibition from 5 nM, indicating that this inhibitor affects GSK3b (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B

claim: LY-213 (B12) reduced pSer222 EB2 at 500 nM but also seemed to decrease β-catenin phosphorylation at this concentration.
source: Finally, LY-213 (B12) reduced pSer222 EB2 at 500 nM but also seemed to decrease β-catenin phosphorylation at this concentration
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Phospho-β-catenin (Ser33/37/Thr41) is reduced upon exposure to GSK3β inhibitor CHIR 99021 while EB2 pSer222 is not affected by GSK3β inhibition.
source: In support of this assay, phospho-β-catenin (Ser33/37/Thr41) is reduced upon exposure to GSK3β inhibitor CHIR 99021 while EB2 pSer222 is not affected by GSK3β inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: CAF-382 (B1) reduced EB2 phosphorylation in hippocampal slices in a dose-dependent fashion.
source: As for primary cultures, CAF-382 (B1) reduced EB2 phosphorylation in a dose-dependent fashion (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6

claim: CAF-382 (B1) at 100 nM reduced EB2 phosphorylation (control: 1 ± 0.10 vs. 100 nM: 0.49 ± 0.02, n = 8, p=0.002, RM-ANOVA).
source: CAF 382 (B1) (control: 1 ± 0.10 vs. 100 nM: 0.49 ± 0.02, n = 8, p=0.002, RM-ANOVA) (control: 1 ± 0.08 vs. 45 nM: 0.16 ± 0.03, n = 10, p<0.001, RM-ANOVA) (control: 1 ± 0.14 vs. 10 nM: 0.62 ± 0.11, n = 7, p=0.003, RM-ANOVA) reduced EB2 phosphorylation at all concentrations
evidence: Supported by quantified western blot data shown in Figure 6B

claim: SNS-032 also reduced EB2 phosphorylation in hippocampal slices.
source: Similarly, SNS-032, the parent compound of CAF-382 (B1), also reduced EB2 phosphorylation in hippocampal slices (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The slope of the input-output relationship was reduced in a dose–response relationship by CAF-382 (B1) within 30 min of application.
source: The slope of this relationship was reduced in a dose–response relationship by CAF-382 (B1) within 30 min of application (Figure 7A)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7A

claim: For a similar input (fiber volley amplitude), the postsynaptic responsiveness (fEPSP slope) was reduced by CAF-382 (B1) in a time- and dose-dependent fashion.
source: In other words, for a similar input (fiber volley amplitude), the postsynaptic responsiveness (fEPSP slope) was reduced (Figure 7B) in a time- and dose-dependent fashion (Figure 7C)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7B and C

claim: CAF-382 (B1) (100 nM) had no effect on the paired-pulse ratio.
source: CAF-382 (B1) (100 nM × 1 hr) had no effect on the paired-pulse ratio, confirming the acute effects of CAF-382 (B1) are restricted to the postsynapse
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8

claim: CAF-382 (B1) did not affect NMDA-receptor-mediated field potential (population spike 2) under conditions with extracellular Mg2+ removed.
source: Under these conditions, an NMDA-receptor-mediated field potential (population spike 2) becomes apparent; this was not affected by CAF-382 (B1) (Figure 9) but was completely blocked by the NMDA-type glutamate receptor antagonist D-APV (50 μM)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 9

claim: CAF-382 (B1) significantly reduced LTP as measured by fEPSP slope at 56–60 min post theta-burst (control: 115.6 ± 2.2 n = 13 slices, 12 rats; CAF-382 (B1): 106.4 ± 3.5, n = 5 slices, four rats; p=0.029, two-way ANOVA, Holm–Sidak post hoc).
source: Compared to interleaved control slices, CAF-382 (B1) significantly reduced LTP as measured by fEPSP slope at 56–60 min post theta-burst (control: 115.6 ± 2.2 n = 13 slices, 12 rats; CAF-382 (B1): 106.4 ± 3.5, n = 5 slices, four rats; p=0.029, two-way ANOVA, Holm–Sidak post hoc)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 10

claim: CAF-382 (B1) significantly reduced LTP of AMPA-type glutamate receptor-mediated synaptic responses at 27–31 min post break-in (control: 197.5 ± 8.4 n = 14 slices, 14 rats; CAF-382 (B1): 123.14 ± 9.0, n = 12–13 slices, 13 rats; p<0.001, two-way ANOVA, Holm–Sidak post hoc).
source: Compared to interleaved control slices, CAF-382 (B1) significantly reduced LTP at 27–31 min post break-in (control: 197.5 ± 8.4 n = 14 slices, 14 rats; CAF-382 (B1): 123.14 ± 9.0, n = 12–13 slices, 13 rats; p<0.001, two-way ANOVA, Holm–Sidak post hoc)
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp data shown in Figure 11

claim: B1 demonstrated good solubility (196 µM).
source: B1 demonstrated good solubility (196 µM), supporting that it readily dissolves in aqueous buffer without observed precipitation
evidence: Supported by kinetic solubility data shown in Table 2

claim: B1 proved to be very tolerant to microsomal exposure and demonstrated excellent stability (>85%) after 30 min.
source: B1 proved to be very tolerant to microsomal exposure, demonstrated excellent stability (>85%) after 30 min, and was not prone to non-NADPH-dependent enzymatic degradation
evidence: Supported by mouse liver microsomal stability data shown in Table 2

claim: The half-life of B1 was found to be <1 hr.
source: The half-life of B1 was found to be <1 hr, with the highest concentration of drug in the plasma found 0.5 hr after dosing (Cmax = 508 ng/mL) and total system exposure (AUCinf) of 646 h*ng/mL (Figure 12)
evidence: Supported by pharmacokinetic data shown in Figure 12

claim: Brain penetration of B1 was generally low.
source: As shown in Table 3, brain and plasma sampling indicated that brain penetration of B1 was generally low
evidence: Supported by brain/plasma concentration data shown in Table 3

claim: Acute inhibition of CDKL5 selectively reduces postsynaptic function of AMPA-type glutamate receptors in a dose-dependent manner in rat hippocampal brain slices.
source: In rat hippocampal brain slices, acute inhibition of CDKL5 selectively reduces postsynaptic function of AMPA-type glutamate receptors in a dose-dependent manner
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 7-9

claim: Acute inhibition of CDKL5 reduces hippocampal LTP.
source: Acute inhibition of CDKL5 reduces hippocampal LTP
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 10-11

claim: CDKL5 kinase function is necessary for synaptic plasticity.
source: These studies provide new tools and insights into the role of CDKL5 as a newly appreciated key kinase necessary for synaptic plasticity
evidence: Inferred from the LTP reduction data shown in Figures 10-11

claim: Compensatory changes have limited the understanding of the roles of CDKL5 in synaptic physiology, plasticity, and human neuropathology.
source: Comparisons to rodent knock-out studies suggest that compensatory changes have limited the understanding of the roles of CDKL5 in synaptic physiology, plasticity, and human neuropathology
evidence: Inferred from comparison of acute inhibition results with genetic knockout studies

claim: The acute effect of CAF-382 (B1)-mediated CDKL5 inhibition is to selectively reduce AMPA-type glutamate receptor-mediated responses postsynaptically.
source: This result suggests that the acute effect of CAF-382 (B1)-mediated CDKL5 inhibition is to selectively reduce AMPA-type glutamate receptor-mediated responses postsynaptically
evidence: Inferred from electrophysiology data showing selective effects on AMPA but not NMDA receptors

claim: CDKL5 has a direct role in the postsynaptic mediation of LTP at Schaffer Collateral to CA1 synapses at P20-30.
source: Since we do not see a presynaptic effect of CAF-382 (B1) (Figure 8), and the approach (Figure 11) removed the contribution of inhibitory synapses, this supports the direct role of CDKL5 in the postsynaptic mediation of LTP at this synapse at this age
evidence: Inferred from combined electrophysiology data showing no presynaptic effects and LTP reduction

claim: Observations of increased LTP in genetic CDKL5 knockout models are compensatory and not directly due to loss of CDKL5.
source: The increased LTP seen in genetic studies suggests that observations of increased LTP in these models are compensatory and not directly due to loss of CDKL5
evidence: Inferred from comparison of acute inhibition results (reduced LTP) with genetic knockout studies (increased LTP)

claim: Synaptic function at P20–30 requires CDKL5 activity for synaptic plasticity.
source: Nevertheless, synaptic function at the developmental age studied (P20–30) requires CDKL5 activity for synaptic plasticity
evidence: Inferred from LTP reduction data at this developmental age

claim: Strategies that boost CDKL5 function at P20-30 age-equivalent in humans may be clinically important.
source: suggesting that strategies that boost function at this age-equivalent in humans may be clinically important
evidence: Speculative inference based on the requirement for CDKL5 in synaptic plasticity at this age

claim: CAF-382 (B1) is one of the best available chemical probes for interrogating CDKL5 activity in vitro.
source: CAF-382 (B1) is one of the best available chemical probes for interrogating CDKL5 activity in vitro, where we envision the greatest utility for future studies
evidence: Inferred from the selectivity and potency data presented throughout the manuscript

claim: CDKL5 inhibition is beneficial for cell survival upon ischemia or nephrotoxin-induced kidney injury.
source: More broadly, CDKL5 inhibition is beneficial for cell survival upon ischemia or nephrotoxin-induced kidney injury (Kim et al., 2020b; Kim et al., 2020a)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in other disease models

claim: Human CDKL5 and rat Cdkl5 isoforms are homologous through the kinase domain.
source: hCDKL5 and rCdkl5 isoforms are homologous through the kinase domain (Hector et al., 2017b; Hector et al., 2016; Hector et al., 2017a)
evidence: Supported by citations to sequence comparison studies

claim: B1 has an IC50 of 6.7 nM in the CDKL5 split-luciferase assay.
evidence: Supported by dose-response curve data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: B4 has an IC50 of 6.4 nM in the CDKL5 split-luciferase assay.
evidence: Supported by dose-response curve data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: B12 has an IC50 of 8.7 nM in the CDKL5 split-luciferase assay.
evidence: Supported by dose-response curve data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A
